tip: Welsh forms the passive with cael ei plus a verb-noun: cael ei thrwsio means is being repaired.
After the feminine ei (its), c, p and t take the aspirate mutation, so cynnal becomes ei chynnal here.
The verb ymweld takes â for what is visited: Ymwelodd hi â'i mam-gu means she visited her grandmother.
Dates use an ordinal with o for of: y pedwerydd o Ebrill means the fourth of April.
Fe'i is the particle fe plus the object pronoun i (him or her): Fe'i penodwyd means he was appointed.
Gwnaed is the irregular impersonal past of gwneud (do or make): Gwnaed y penderfyniad means the decision was made.
The -wyd ending is the impersonal past, a passive with no named doer: Sefydlwyd yr ysgol means the school was founded.
To name the doer after an impersonal verb, add gan (by): gan Aneirin means by Aneirin.
The object of an inflected verb takes the soft mutation: tractor becomes dractor in Prynodd Iolo dractor newydd.
After fy (my), g nasal-mutates to ng: goruchwyliwr becomes fy ngoruchwyliwr.
Pe bai plus wedi makes a past unreal: Pe bai'r polisi wedi'i weithredu means if the policy had been implemented.
Welsh has no plain verb to need. Mae angen plus a verb-noun does it: Mae angen gweithredu means action is needed.
Ordinals agree with feminine nouns: trydydd (third) becomes drydedd in y drydedd ganrif.
Cafodd plus ei plus a verb-noun is the past passive: Cafodd y bont ei difrodi means the bridge was damaged.
The -wch ending makes a plural or polite command: Paratowch means prepare (you).
A verb-noun can act as a subject like an -ing noun: Mae teithio'n ehangu means travelling broadens.
After masculine ei (his), t softens to d: traethawd becomes ei draethawd.
Mae plus yn plus a verb-noun is the present tense: Mae'r myfyrwyr yn astudio means the students study.
Feminine ei adds h to a word starting with a vowel: adeiladu becomes ei hadeiladu.
Feminine nouns soft-mutate after the article yr or 'r: prifysgol becomes i'r brifysgol here.
gan softens the word after it: Llywodraeth becomes gan Lywodraeth.
